source_passages.quote: the attribute values xi are conditionally independent of each other, given the class label y
supports: definition of the naive independence assumption

source_passages.quote: P(x|y) can be factored as a product of class-conditional probabilities of every attribute
can produce incorrect results when the attributes are not conditionally independent given the class labels

reference_text: The naive independence assumption is the simplifying assumption used by the naïve Bayes classifier to make class-conditional probability estimation tractable. Given a class label, the attribute values are treated as conditionally independent of one another. Under this assumption, the joint class-conditional probability of an instance can be factored into a product of the separate class-conditional probabilities for its individual attributes. Conditioning is essential: the attributes need not be independent in the data overall; the assumption is that once the class is known, knowing one attribute does not change the conditional distribution of another. This factorization avoids having to estimate probabilities for every combination of attribute values, which becomes difficult as the number of attributes grows. The assumption is nevertheless an approximation. When attributes remain dependent within a class, especially when they are redundant or interact, naïve Bayes can produce incorrect posterior probabilities and classifications.

source_passages.quote: We can check the correlation between them using the χ2 test.
The χ2 value ... is computed as ... (oij − eij)² / eij
The χ2 test checks the hypothesis that A and B are independent

reference_text: The chi-squared test is a dependence test used in the corpus to determine whether two nominal attributes are statistically related. The values of the two attributes are first arranged in a contingency table whose cells contain observed joint-event frequencies. For each cell, an expected frequency is computed from the corresponding marginal counts under the assumption that the attributes are independent. The Pearson chi-squared statistic then sums the squared differences between observed and expected frequencies, divided by the expected frequencies, across all cells. If the attributes have c and r distinct values, the test uses (c−1)(r−1) degrees of freedom. The resulting statistic or significance level is compared with the chosen significance criterion. A sufficiently large chi-squared statistic, equivalently a sufficiently small significance probability, leads to rejection of the null hypothesis of independence and supports the conclusion that the attributes are statistically correlated. Thus the test measures departure from independence rather than merely raw co-occurrence.

source_passages.quote: It cannot handle non-globular clusters or clusters of different sizes and densities
K-means also has trouble clustering data that contains outliers.
K-means is restricted to data for which there is a notion of a center

reference_text: K-means has important limitations that follow from the kind of clusters and data representation it assumes. Although it is simple and efficient, it is not suitable for all cluster structures. In particular, the corpus states that it cannot properly handle non-globular clusters or clusters that differ substantially in size or density. With a sufficiently large requested number of clusters it may find pure subclusters, but those subclusters need not coincide with the natural groups in the data. K-means also has difficulty when outliers are present, because unusual points can adversely affect the clustering; detecting and removing outliers can therefore help. A further restriction is that K-means requires data for which a meaningful center or centroid can be defined. This distinguishes it from related approaches such as K-medoids, which remove that centroid requirement at greater computational cost. These limitations mean that K-means suitability depends on the geometry and representation of the data, not merely on choosing K.

source_passages.quote: The filter approach operates independently of the DM method subsequently employed.
the wrapper approach uses a learning algorithm as a black box together with statistical validation
when data size is huge, the wrapper approach cannot be applied

reference_text: The filter-versus-wrapper trade-off concerns how feature subsets are evaluated and the consequences of that choice. Filter methods evaluate features using criteria such as information, distance, dependence, or consistency independently of the learning algorithm that will later use the selected features. Because these criteria are generally cheaper than repeatedly measuring predictive accuracy, filters are usually faster, scale to larger data sets, and produce feature subsets that are not tied to one particular learner. Wrapper methods instead use a learning algorithm itself as a black-box evaluator, typically with statistical validation such as cross-validation, and search for the subset that gives the strongest predictive performance for that fixed learner. This lets wrappers exploit the learning algorithm's particular bias, which filters cannot do, but it requires repeated model training and is consequently much more expensive. The corpus therefore presents a clear trade-off: filters emphasize efficiency, scalability, and learner independence, whereas wrappers emphasize learner-specific predictive performance at greater computational cost and with a stronger need to control overfitting.

source_passages.quote: an ideal cluster similarity matrix has a block diagonal structure
assigning a 1 to an entry if the associated pair of points belongs to the same cluster
the patterns displayed in the similarity matrix can reveal the relationships between clusters

reference_text: A similarity matrix records pairwise similarities among data objects, with one row and one column for each object. In cluster evaluation, the matrix can be reordered so that objects assigned to the same cluster are adjacent. For an ideal clustering, the corresponding ideal similarity matrix has a block-diagonal structure: entries representing pairs within the same cluster are assigned similarity 1, while entries for pairs in different clusters are 0. An actual reordered similarity matrix for well-separated clusters should show a strong approximate block-diagonal pattern. Comparing the actual and ideal matrices, or simply inspecting the reordered actual matrix, provides information about cluster quality and relationships among clusters. Strong within-block similarity and weak between-block similarity are characteristic of well-separated groups, whereas weaker or irregular block patterns can indicate less distinct structure. The same qualitative reasoning can be applied to dissimilarity matrices. Computing the full pairwise proximity matrix is quadratic in the number of objects, so sampling can be used for large data sets.

source_passages.quote: the training error rate ... can under-estimate gen.error(m) when the model complexity is high
gen.error(m)=train.error(m, D.train)+α×complexity(M)
Models that deliver such predictive insights are said to have good generalization performance.

reference_text: Generalization error is the error associated with a model's performance on previously unseen data, rather than merely on the examples used to build the model. The corpus emphasizes that training error can underestimate this error when model complexity is high, because a complex model can fit peculiarities of the training sample that do not persist on new instances. One generic way presented for estimating generalization error adds a complexity penalty to training error: the estimate is training error plus a tunable coefficient multiplied by model complexity. The coefficient controls the trade-off between fitting the training data and preferring a simpler model. For decision trees, one proposed complexity measure is the number of leaf nodes relative to the number of training instances. This makes generalization error central to model selection and pruning: reducing training error alone is not sufficient if the additional structure increases complexity enough to worsen expected performance on new data. Independent test data provide a direct basis for evaluating this generalization performance.

source_passages.quote: many types of data analysis become significantly harder as the dimensionality of the data increases
as dimensionality increases, the data becomes increasingly sparse in the space that it occupies
the differences in density and in the distances between points ... become less meaningful

reference_text: The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon that many forms of data analysis become substantially harder as the number of attributes increases. The corpus explains the central mechanism in terms of sparsity: as dimensionality grows, observed data occupy an increasingly small and sparse portion of the possible space. Consequently, the available objects may no longer be representative of the range of objects that could occur. For classification, this can leave too few observations to construct a model that reliably assigns classes throughout the input space. For clustering, quantities that many algorithms depend on, especially local density and differences in distances between points, become less informative. Dimensionality reduction is therefore useful not only for reducing computation and memory but also for counteracting these analytical difficulties. Feature selection addresses dimensionality by retaining a subset of the original attributes, while other dimensionality-reduction methods may construct new attributes. The key issue is thus not simply computational cost; increasing dimension changes how well finite data represent the space and how meaningful proximity structure remains.

source_passages.quote: The min-max normalization aims to scale all the numerical values ... to a specified range
avoid those attributes with a large ... difference dominating over the other ones in the distance calculation
Data transformation usually combines the original raw attributes using different mathematical formulas

reference_text: Normalization and transformation modify the representation of data so that it is better suited to a later data-mining method. Normalization changes the numerical scale or distribution of existing attributes without necessarily creating new attributes. Min-max normalization, for example, maps values from their original range to a specified new interval, commonly [0,1]. Putting attributes on comparable ranges is especially important for distance-based methods because an attribute with a much larger numerical range can otherwise dominate a distance calculation; normalization can also accelerate learning in neural networks. The corpus also describes z-score normalization, which centers an attribute and scales it by its standard deviation, and decimal scaling. Data transformation is broader: it can combine original attributes through mathematical formulas to construct derived attributes. Linear and quadratic transformations are examples, and the resulting attributes may expose structure that is not apparent in the original variables. Thus normalization primarily rescales existing values, whereas transformation can change the feature representation itself to make a mining task more effective.

source_passages.quote: the training set ... contains attribute values as well as class labels for each instance
supports: role of the class label in training

source_passages.quote: applying the model to assign labels to unlabeled instances
the attributes are influenced only by the target class

reference_text: The target attribute in a classification problem is the outcome that the classifier is intended to predict. The course corpus expresses this idea primarily using the terms class label and target class. A training set contains ordinary attribute values together with a class label for each instance, and a learning algorithm uses those labeled examples to construct a classification model. The learned model is then applied to previously unlabeled instances to predict their class labels. The target therefore differs from the input attributes: the inputs describe an instance, while the target supplies the category that the learning process is trying to infer from those inputs. This distinction also appears in the naïve Bayes discussion, where the class is explicitly called the target class and the other attributes are modeled conditionally on it. The target attribute is consequently the supervised output variable that defines what the classification task is trying to learn and what predictions are evaluated against on unseen data.
notes: The corpus mostly uses “class label” and “target class” rather than the exact phrase “target attribute”; the description stays within that source terminology.

unsupported_reason: The attached course corpus does not define Spearman rank correlation, give its coefficient or ranking procedure, or distinguish it from other correlation measures. Generic references to rank correlation are insufficient to reconstruct this specific concept without outside knowledge.

source_passages.quote: every neighbor has the same impact on the classification
predicts the class label of a test instance by taking a majority vote
a weighted majority vote ... can be used to combine the predictions

reference_text: Majority voting is a rule for combining multiple class predictions by selecting the class that receives the largest number of votes. In the ensemble setting described in the corpus, each base classifier produces a predicted class for a test instance, and the ensemble prediction is obtained from the majority of those predictions. The same principle appears in k-nearest-neighbor classification: each of the selected neighbors contributes one equal vote, and the class with the largest vote count is chosen. Equal voting distinguishes ordinary majority voting from weighted voting, where predictions are given different influence. For example, distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting gives closer neighbors more influence, and boosting combines classifiers with weights related to their performance rather than treating every classifier identically. Majority voting is therefore a simple aggregation mechanism rather than a training procedure by itself. Its behavior depends on the quality and diversity of the individual voters, while alternative weighted schemes modify the equal-contribution assumption when some voters should have greater influence than others.

unsupported_reason: No substantive definition, procedure, formula, or interpretation of the Nemenyi test was found in the attached course corpus. Writing one would require information external to the permitted sources.

source_passages.quote: Start with one, all-inclusive cluster and, at each step, split a cluster
until only singleton clusters of individual points remain
the order in which the clusters were ... split (divisive view)

reference_text: Divisive, or top-down, hierarchical clustering constructs a hierarchy by repeatedly splitting clusters. It begins with one all-inclusive cluster containing every data object. At each subsequent step, one existing cluster is selected and divided, and this process can continue until the hierarchy reaches singleton clusters containing individual objects. Two choices are therefore central to a divisive method: deciding which current cluster should be split next and deciding how that split should be performed. This direction is the reverse of agglomerative hierarchical clustering, which starts from singleton clusters and repeatedly merges the closest pair. Both approaches produce a hierarchy rather than only one flat partition. The resulting cluster-subcluster relationships can be represented with a dendrogram. In the divisive interpretation of a dendrogram, the diagram records the order in which clusters were split. The course text notes that agglomerative methods are more common, but the defining distinction is clear: divisive clustering proceeds from one broad cluster downward toward progressively finer groups.

unsupported_reason: The attached corpus does not define mean absolute error as an evaluation measure for ordinal classification targets, nor does it specify how ordinal class distances are encoded for MAE. An unrelated mean-absolute-deviation formula in normalization does not support this KC.

source_passages.quote: r=1. City block (Manhattan, taxicab, L1 norm) distance.
specify different ways of combining the differences in each dimension ... into an overall distance
for Manhattan (L1) distance ... the appropriate centroid is the median

reference_text: Manhattan distance is the r=1 case of the Minkowski family of distances and is also called city-block, taxicab, or L1 distance. For two objects represented by numerical attribute vectors, it combines their coordinate-wise differences by taking the absolute difference on each attribute and summing those absolute differences. This differs from Euclidean distance, the r=2 Minkowski case, which combines squared differences and then takes a square root. The Manhattan measure is defined for any number of dimensions and provides one way of turning differences across individual attributes into a single overall dissimilarity. The clustering discussion shows that the choice of distance also affects what constitutes an appropriate cluster center and objective. When Manhattan distance is used with the objective of minimizing the total distance from objects to their cluster center, the appropriate centroid representative is the median rather than the mean. Thus Manhattan distance is not simply another name for Euclidean distance; it embodies a distinct L1 geometry with different optimization consequences.

source_passages.quote: The first two cases result in “one-sided tests”
the last case results in a “two-sided test.”
greater than or equal to ... RH, smaller than or equal to ... RL, or outside ... [RL,RH]

reference_text: One-sided and two-sided tests differ in which parts of a test statistic's null distribution are treated as sufficiently extreme evidence against the null hypothesis. The corpus describes three possibilities for an observed statistic: it may be extreme when it is at least a high critical value, when it is at most a low critical value, or when it falls outside a central interval bounded by low and high critical values. The first two choices produce one-sided tests. A right-tailed test looks for unusually large values, while a left-tailed test looks for unusually small values. The third choice produces a two-sided test because extreme outcomes in either direction can count against the null hypothesis. The distinction is therefore determined by how “extreme” is defined for the statistic under the hypotheses, not by a different general testing framework. In either case, the test statistic is interpreted relative to its null distribution; the difference is whether evidence is collected from one tail or from both tails.

source_passages.quote: information gain ... is defined as the difference between the prior uncertainty ... and the expected posterior uncertainty
Ai is chosen instead of Aj if IG(Ai) > IG(Aj)
Information gain has a tendency to choose features with more distinct values.
supports: known bias and contrast with gain ratio

reference_text: Information gain measures how much uncertainty about the class is reduced by using a feature to partition the data. The corpus defines it as the prior class uncertainty minus the expected posterior uncertainty after the values of a feature are taken into account. When Shannon entropy is used as the uncertainty function, the information at the parent data set is compared with the size-weighted entropy of the partitions produced by the candidate feature. A feature with larger information gain produces a larger reduction in class uncertainty and is therefore preferred to one with smaller gain. This principle is used for feature evaluation and for selecting branching attributes in decision-tree induction. Information gain has an important limitation: it tends to favor features having many distinct values, because such features can create highly pure partitions even when those partitions are not useful for generalization. The corpus therefore introduces gain ratio as a way to compensate for this preference. Information gain should consequently be understood as an entropy-reduction criterion whose raw value can be biased toward highly partitioning attributes.

source_passages.quote: Each point along the curve corresponds to a classification model generated by placing a threshold on the test scores
This approach is equivalent to classifying all the test instances as positive class.
Repeat Step 3 and update the TP and FP counts accordingly until the highest ranked test instance is selected.

reference_text: A classification threshold, or cutoff, converts a continuous classifier score into a class decision. In the ROC-analysis procedure described in the corpus, test instances are ordered by their scores and a threshold is placed on those scores. Instances on the positive side of the cutoff are classified as positive and the others as negative. Changing the threshold changes the entries of the confusion matrix, and therefore changes the true-positive and false-positive rates. At the lowest threshold all test instances are classified as positive. As the threshold is raised, instances are progressively moved to the negative prediction side; at the other extreme, all are classified as negative. Each threshold setting therefore corresponds to a point on the ROC curve. The cutoff is not a fixed property of the scoring model itself. It is an operating choice that determines the trade-off between different kinds of classification outcomes. ROC analysis evaluates the classifier over this range of possible thresholds rather than at only one arbitrarily chosen cutoff.

source_passages.quote: simply using the training error rate as an estimate ... is called the optimistic error estimate
or the resubstitution estimate
the training error rate ... can under-estimate gen.error(m) when the model complexity is high

reference_text: The optimistic error estimate is the practice of using a model's training error rate directly as an estimate of its generalization error. The course text also calls this the resubstitution estimate. It is described as optimistic because the same data used to construct the model are used to assess its error, so the resulting value can make future performance look better than it really is. This problem is particularly important for complex models: training error can underestimate generalization error when the model has enough flexibility to fit peculiarities of the training sample. The corpus contrasts the optimistic estimate with a pessimistic error estimate for decision trees. The pessimistic approach adds a penalty for model complexity, such as a cost related to the number of leaf nodes relative to the training-set size, and therefore assumes generalization error will be worse than raw training error. The optimistic estimate is consequently simple, but it provides no correction for complexity or reuse of the training data and can favor an overfitted tree.

source_passages.quote: Exhaustive methods cover the whole search space.
there should be a total of 2M subsets where M is the number of features
the number of possibilities is prohibitive

reference_text: Exhaustive search in feature selection means considering the complete feature-subset search space rather than following only a restricted heuristic path through it. With M original features, the subset space contains 2^M possible subsets, so complete exploration can become extremely expensive as dimensionality increases. The feature-selection chapter classifies exhaustive methods as approaches that cover the whole search space. One described strategy examines combinations according to subset size and evaluates whether a candidate subset satisfies the chosen criterion, such as consistency, with the goal of finding a smallest satisfactory subset. The benefit of exhaustive search is completeness: because the search is not restricted to locally promising additions or removals, the desired subset is not excluded merely by the direction of a greedy procedure. Its central cost is combinatorial growth. The corpus explicitly notes that the number of possibilities can become prohibitive when the desired subset is not small. Exhaustive approaches are therefore conceptually thorough but computationally limited, motivating complete methods with pruning as well as heuristic and stochastic alternatives.

source_passages.quote: For a multiway split ... the number of outcomes depends on the number of distinct values
its test condition will produce a three-way split
having more number of child nodes can make a decision tree more complex

reference_text: A bushy, or multi-split, decision-tree structure arises when a node can create more than two child branches from one attribute test. The corpus explains this directly for nominal attributes: a multiway split creates a number of outcomes determined by the number of distinct attribute values. An attribute with three values, for example, can produce a three-way split. This contrasts with binary splitting, where the values are partitioned into only two groups and every internal node has two outcomes. Multiway splitting can make training partitions very pure, but the text warns that attributes with many distinct values can create many child nodes, making the tree more complex and more susceptible to overfitting. An extreme example is an attribute with a unique value for each training instance, which can perfectly separate the training data but does not generalize usefully to unseen values. This is why some tree algorithms, such as CART, restrict themselves to binary splits, while other criteria such as gain ratio compensate for attributes that generate many partitions.
notes: The source explains multiway splitting and its complexity consequences but does not use “bushy decision tree” as the primary label.

source_passages.quote: Classification error = 1 − max_i[p_i(t)]
The impurity of a node measures how dissimilar the class labels are
Calculate the weighted misclassification rate of the child nodes.

reference_text: Misclassification rate is used in the decision-tree material as a node-impurity and split-evaluation measure. For a node t, the classification error is defined as one minus the largest class proportion at that node, 1−max_i p_i(t). The majority class is the class with the largest p_i(t), so this quantity is the fraction of instances that would be misclassified if the node were labeled with that majority class. A pure node has all of its instances in one class and therefore has zero classification error. A more mixed node produces a larger value because a larger fraction falls outside its dominant class. When considering a split, the misclassification rates of the child nodes can be combined in a size-weighted way and compared with the parent-node impurity to judge whether the split improves class separation. The measure is one of several impurity criteria discussed for decision trees, alongside entropy and the Gini index. Its interpretation is directly tied to the errors incurred by majority-class labeling at a node.

source_passages.quote: There are two ways to estimate the class-conditional probabilities for continuous attributes
we can use a Gaussian distribution to represent the conditional probability of continuous attributes
The Gaussian distribution is characterized by two parameters, the mean, μ, and the variance, σ2.
supports: parameters estimated per class and attribute

reference_text: Naïve Bayes can handle numerical, continuous attributes by modeling their class-conditional probabilities rather than requiring the attributes to be categorical. The corpus presents two main strategies. One is to discretize a continuous attribute into intervals and then use the categorical probability-estimation procedure. The other is to assume a parametric probability distribution for the continuous values and estimate that distribution from the training data. Gaussian naïve Bayes is the example given for the second strategy. For each numerical attribute and each class, the conditional distribution is represented by a Gaussian characterized by a class-specific mean and variance estimated from the training examples. A test value is then assigned a class-conditional likelihood using the Gaussian density with those parameters, and these attribute likelihoods participate in the usual naïve Bayes calculation. The approach therefore replaces frequency counts for exact continuous values with a smooth probabilistic model. Its validity depends on the chosen distribution being a reasonable representation of the attribute values within each class; discretization is an alternative when that modeling assumption is not desired.

source_passages.quote: Here we discuss methods for estimating its generalization performance, i.e. its performance on unseen instances outside of D.train.
a labeled test set has not been used at any stage of model selection
one of the partitions ... is chosen ... for testing, while the rest ... are used ... for training

reference_text: The evaluation workflow separates learning and model selection from the final assessment of generalization performance. The corpus defines model evaluation as estimating how a model performs on previously unseen data. Training error alone is not sufficient, and even performance on validation data used to choose among models or hyperparameters is an optimistically biased estimate of the selected model's final performance because the selection decision has already depended on that data. A correct workflow therefore keeps labeled evaluation data independent from the choices used to construct the final model. In a holdout design, data are divided into training, validation, and test roles: training builds candidate models, validation supports model selection, and the final test set is used only after the selection is complete. When labeled data are limited, cross-validation repeatedly rotates training and test folds to estimate generalization performance more efficiently. The essential principle is that the evidence used for final evaluation must not be the same evidence that directly determined the chosen model, otherwise the reported performance becomes biased toward that choice.

source_passages.quote: we can try to evaluate whether a data set has clusters without clustering
The most common approach ... has been to use statistical tests for spatial randomness.
If the randomly generated points and the sample of data points have roughly the same nearest neighbor distances, then H will be near 0.5.

reference_text: The corpus supports a randomness-based approach to assessing clustering tendency, although it does not label or number it explicitly as “Models of Randomness (Approach 1).” The underlying idea is to ask whether a data set shows evidence of cluster structure before committing to a clustering result. Because ordinary clustering algorithms can return clusters even for random data, clustering tendency can instead be evaluated using statistical tests for spatial randomness. The text notes that this requires a model of randomness, parameter choices, and a significance assessment, all of which can be challenging. Its concrete example is the Hopkins statistic. Random points are generated in the data space and actual data points are sampled; nearest-neighbor distances for the two groups are compared. If the two sets of distances are similar, the Hopkins statistic is near 0.5, consistent with spatial randomness. Values far from that random pattern indicate non-random spatial structure. This supports the general randomness-model mechanism, but not the exact “Approach 1” taxonomy implied by the KC name.
notes: PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED because the corpus clearly explains statistical models/tests of spatial randomness and Hopkins clustering tendency, but does not identify a named or numbered category called “Models of Randomness (Approach 1).”

source_passages.quote: a tree-like diagram called a dendrogram
displays both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which the clusters were merged
or split (divisive view)

reference_text: A dendrogram is a tree-like graphical representation of a hierarchical clustering. It displays not only which objects or clusters are grouped within larger clusters, but also the hierarchical sequence in which those groupings were formed. In an agglomerative interpretation, the dendrogram records the order in which smaller clusters were merged as the algorithm proceeds from individual points toward larger groups. In a divisive interpretation, it records the reverse type of process: how an initially broad cluster is successively split into smaller clusters. The branches therefore encode cluster-subcluster relationships across multiple levels rather than showing only one flat partition of the data. This is what makes the dendrogram useful for understanding hierarchical methods: a single diagram preserves the nested organization produced throughout the clustering process. The corpus contrasts this tree representation with a nested-cluster diagram for two-dimensional examples, but the dendrogram is the general tree-form visualization associated with hierarchical clustering and can represent either the agglomerative or divisive direction.

source_passages.quote: This information can be summarized in a table called a confusion matrix.
Each entry fij denotes the number of instances from class i predicted to be of class j.
A confusion matrix summarizes the number of instances predicted correctly or incorrectly by a classifier

reference_text: The course corpus defines the general cell semantics of a confusion matrix but illustrates them explicitly only for binary classification, so support for a specifically multi-class confusion matrix is incomplete. A confusion matrix is a table that compares true class membership with classifier predictions. Its entry f_ij denotes the number of instances whose actual class is i but whose predicted class is j. Entries where the predicted class matches the actual class represent correct predictions, while off-diagonal entries represent particular kinds of misclassification. This organization makes the matrix more informative than a single overall accuracy value because it preserves which classes are being confused with which others. The later classifier-evaluation discussion again uses a binary confusion matrix to separate true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. The f_ij definition is compatible with more than two class labels, but the attached corpus does not explicitly present or discuss the full multi-class matrix, its dimensions, or multi-class-specific summaries. A stronger multi-class description would therefore require inference beyond the supplied text.
notes: PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED because the corpus supplies general f_ij cell semantics but its worked classifier confusion matrices are explicitly binary; it does not separately define a multi-class confusion matrix.

source_passages.quote: a sample is representative if it has approximately the same property ... as the original set of data
choose a sampling scheme that guarantees a high probability of getting a representative sample
The model is created using ... the training set
supports: role of the training sample in classification

reference_text: A representative training sample is a training set whose relevant properties sufficiently reflect those of the larger population or data set from which future instances arise. The sampling chapter states the general principle directly: a sample is representative when it has approximately the same property of interest as the original data. Which property matters depends on the analysis; for example, if the mean is important, a representative sample should have a mean close to that of the full data. Because sampling is stochastic, no particular sample is guaranteed to be perfectly representative, so the sampling method and sample size should be chosen to give a high probability of obtaining an adequate sample. In classification, the training set is the labeled data used to construct the model. Representativeness therefore matters because the learned classifier can only learn patterns exposed by its training examples. A training sample that does not reflect the relevant distribution of the broader data can lead to a model whose apparent training performance does not translate to unseen instances.

source_passages.quote: It is also possible to create a binary split by partitioning all values ... into two groups.
some decision tree algorithms, such as CART, produce only binary splits
One way is to generate only binary decision trees
supports: motivation and contrast with multiway trees

reference_text: A binary decision tree is a decision tree whose internal test conditions produce two child outcomes rather than a larger multiway set of branches. For a nominal attribute with several possible values, a binary split can be formed by partitioning those values into two groups. This contrasts with a multiway split, where the number of children may follow the number of distinct attribute values. The corpus identifies CART as an example of a decision-tree method that produces only binary splits. Restricting a tree to binary splits also addresses a model-selection problem created by attributes with many values. Such attributes can generate many child nodes and can appear artificially attractive under impurity-reduction criteria because they partition the training data very finely, increasing tree complexity and susceptibility to overfitting. Using only binary decision trees makes the number of outcomes at each split consistent, avoiding direct comparison among candidate attributes that create very different numbers of partitions. Thus “binary” refers to the branching structure at each internal node, not to the number of target classes.

source_passages.quote: segmenting the labeled data D ... into k equal-sized partitions (or folds)
one of the partitions ... is chosen ... for testing, while the rest ... are used ... for training
Every instance in the data is thus used for testing exactly once

reference_text: k-fold cross-validation estimates generalization performance by repeatedly training and testing on different parts of the same labeled data set. The data are divided into k approximately equal folds. On run i, one fold is reserved as the test set and the remaining k−1 folds are used to train a model. This is repeated k times so that every fold serves as the test fold once. The test errors from all runs are aggregated, and every instance is used for testing exactly once and for training k−1 times. The choice of k creates a trade-off. Smaller k means each model is trained on a smaller fraction of the available data, which can increase bias in the estimated generalization error. Larger k leaves more data for training but requires more repeated model fitting. The limiting case k=N is leave-one-out cross-validation, where each run tests on one instance; it can be computationally expensive and does not provide multiple distinct partitionings for estimating variance. The text identifies values around 5 to 10 as a practical choice in many applications and also describes stratified cross-validation for preserving class proportions across folds.
